sections.h2: How is Ohio organized when you sell a house?
sections.html:
Ohio has 88 counties, and the county is where most of the paperwork for a house sale happens. The Wikipedia county list shows Noble County, created in 1851, as the newest one. Each county has its own auditor, treasurer and recorder, so the office you call depends on the parcel, not on the city name in the mailing address.

Cities sit inside counties. Under the state's municipality list, a municipality with at least 5,000 people is a city and a smaller one is a village. Several cities share a name with their county (Delaware, Marion, Athens, Medina), so double check which office you are calling.

The county sections further down group our city and county guides the same way. If you are not sure which county a house is in, check the property tax bill or ask the county auditor's office. For a wider list of local guides, see our Ohio guides by city and county.

sections.h2: What fees and deadlines apply to an Ohio sale?
sections.html:
Most Ohio costs at the county level are small and rule based, though a few depend on where the house sits. The table collects the ones we confirmed from the Ohio Revised Code (ORC).

ItemRuleWhere it comes from
Conveyance fee$1 or 10 cents per $100 of value, whichever is greaterORC 319.54(G)(3)
Who pays itThe seller (grantor), plus any county transfer taxORC 319.202
Optional county transfer taxUp to 30 cents per $100 of valueORC 322.02
Valuation complaintFile with the auditor by March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever is laterORC 5715.19
Sheriff sale floorTwo-thirds of appraised value, with listed exceptionsORC 2329.20
Month-to-month lease endNotice at least 30 days before the rental dateORC 5321.17
Small estate releaseAssets of $35,000 or less, or $100,000 with a spouse and other conditionsORC 2113.03

Whether your county adds the optional transfer tax is not something we could confirm for all 88 counties, so ask the county auditor before you budget. Our Ohio closing costs guide walks through the same fee in more detail.

sections.h2: Who do I call about property tax and recording in Ohio?
sections.html:
Three county offices handle nearly everything. Each is a separate door, and they do not always share the same hours or phone system.

  • County auditor. Takes valuation complaints, homestead applications and the statement of value that is filed before a deed is recorded.
  • County treasurer. Collects the tax bill and takes payment to redeem delinquent land.
  • County recorder. Records the deed. Under ORC 5301.25, a deed must be recorded in the county where the property lies, and an unrecorded deed is fraudulent as to a later buyer who had no knowledge of it.

Due dates are local. Franklin County lists its first half as February 28 and its second half as July 20. In 2026 Cuyahoga County announced that a change in state law pushed its second-half deadline to August 13. Those two examples show why a bill from another county tells you little. Read your own bill or call the treasurer.

Our county pages cover these offices one county at a time and are linked under each county heading below. The statewide version is in the Ohio property tax guide.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in Ohio?
sections.html:
Ohio foreclosure goes through the courts. A mortgage foreclosure ends with a sale ordered by the court (ORC 2323.07), and in practice that means a sheriff sale.

A few rules matter to a homeowner who is weighing a sale against a sale by the sheriff:

  • The sale notice must be published once a week for at least three consecutive weeks, and the owner must be served with written notice.
  • Land generally cannot sell for less than two-thirds of its appraised value.
  • The court has 30 days after the writ is returned to confirm the sale, unless it stays confirmation.
  • The debtor can redeem at any time before confirmation by depositing the judgment, costs and interest at 8 percent a year on the purchase money.

Unpaid property tax has its own track. Delinquent land can be redeemed before foreclosure starts, and after it starts, until the court confirms the sale (ORC 5721.25). Payment goes to the county treasurer. A sale transfer made for delinquent taxes does not carry the auditor's conveyance fee.

We did not find a single statewide timeline from first missed payment to sale, so ask the clerk of courts in your county. Details are in our Ohio sheriff sale guide and tax lien guide.

sections.h2: What happens when you inherit a house in Ohio?
sections.html:
Inherited Ohio homes are handled through the county probate court. Not every estate needs full administration. Under ORC 2113.03, the court may release an estate from administration when assets are $35,000 or less. The ceiling is $100,000 when the decedent left everything to a surviving spouse and other conditions are met.

Ohio also lets an owner name a beneficiary for real estate with a transfer on death designation affidavit. It must be recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies, and title vests in the beneficiary at death without a probate sale (ORC 5302.22).

Two cost points help heirs. A transfer among heirs or devisees for no money is exempt from the conveyance fee. And a fiduciary selling during estate administration, or an heir who inherited and did not live in the home in the past year, does not have to give the standard seller disclosure form. Ohio repealed its estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2013, per the Department of Taxation.

For step-by-step help, read our Ohio probate guide, the page on the transfer on death affidavit and the note on the estate tax repeal.

sections.h2: Does the Ohio homestead exemption affect a sale?
sections.html:
It can change the tax bill you carry until the closing, though it does not block a sale. Ohio's homestead reduction is for owner-occupied homes, covers up to one acre of surrounding land, and is limited to certain people. ORC 323.151 lists age 65 and older, permanently and totally disabled owners, and disabled veterans and their surviving spouses.

Limits change. The Geauga County auditor's 2026 page lists income under $41,000 for newly applying seniors and disabled owners, with the first $29,000 of market value exempt, and a December 31 filing deadline for real property. Those are one auditor's figures, so check your own county.

Our Ohio homestead exemption guide covers eligibility and filing.

sections.h2: What about tenants in a house you want to sell?
sections.html:
Ohio puts a few firm timelines on ending a tenancy. For a month-to-month lease, either side must give notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date, and for week-to-week it is seven days (ORC 5321.17). Before an eviction case can be filed, the party must give the other a notice to leave at least three days before filing. It can go by certified mail, by hand, or by leaving it at the home (ORC 1923.04).

What we could not confirm is whether a sale by itself ends a lease, so ask a real estate attorney before you promise a buyer vacant possession. Sellers with a tenant have a few choices:

  • Sell with the tenant in place, if the buyer is fine with that.
  • Serve the proper notice and sell once the home is empty.
  • Agree on a move-out date with the tenant in writing.

Our landlord and tenant guide, the eviction notice page and the eviction process page cover the steps in more detail.

sections.h2: What does an as-is cash sale mean in Ohio?
sections.html:
It means you sell the house in its current condition and the buyer pays cash instead of relying on a lender. In Ohio, an as-is price does not erase every disclosure duty. A person transferring a one to four unit home by sale must complete the state disclosure form and give a copy to the buyer or the buyer's agent (ORC 5302.30). Exemptions include court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales and fiduciaries in an estate, as noted above.

The deed still has to be signed, acknowledged and recorded, and the auditor still needs the statement of value. How a closing runs, and whether an attorney or a title company leads it, varies, and we did not find an official statewide rule, so ask the title company or your own lawyer what they require.

Property condition is the other question. The EPA says to test every home for radon no matter where it sits, and to fix a home at 4 pCi/L or higher. Its Ohio zone map dates to 1993 and is not meant to decide whether one house needs a test. See our land contract guide if the house is tied up in an installment sale.

faqs.q: How many counties does Ohio have?
faqs.a: Ohio has 88 counties. Each has its own auditor, treasurer and recorder, so tax and deed questions go to the county where the house sits.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance fee when I sell?
faqs.a: In Ohio the seller (grantor) pays the mandatory conveyance fee, which is $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value, whichever is greater. A county may add a transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100, so ask the auditor for your county.

Yes. A court orders the sale, and sheriff sale notice runs once a week for at least three weeks. You can redeem before the court confirms the sale by paying the judgment, costs and 8 percent interest.

faqs.q: Does an inherited house have to go through probate?
faqs.a: Not always. The court may release a small estate from administration at $35,000 or less in assets, or $100,000 with a surviving spouse and other conditions. A recorded transfer on death affidavit also passes title without probate.

faqs.q: How much notice does a month-to-month tenant get?
faqs.a: The landlord or the tenant must give notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date. Before an eviction can be filed, a separate notice to leave must go out at least three days earlier.

faqs.q: Do I still fill out a disclosure form in a cash sale?
faqs.a: Usually yes for a one to four unit home, with exemptions for foreclosure sales, court-ordered transfers, fiduciaries and some heirs. Ask an attorney about your case.

faqs.q: When are Ohio property taxes due?
faqs.a: Dates are set by county. Franklin County lists February 28 and July 20, and Cuyahoga County set August 13 for its 2026 second half. Check your own bill or call your county treasurer.
